{{Short description|Type of ordinary differential equation}}
{{distinguish|text = [[d'Alembert's principle]], [[d'Alembert's formula]] or the [[d'Alembert operator]]}}
{{one source |date=April 2024}}
In [[mathematics]], '''d'Alembert's equation''', sometimes also known as '''Lagrange's equation''',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=d'Alembert's Equation |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ |access-date=2024-06-02 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref> is a first order nonlinear [[ordinary differential equation]], named after the French mathematician [[Jean le Rond d'Alembert]]. The equation reads as<ref>Davis, Harold Thayer. Introduction to nonlinear differential and integral equations. Courier Corporation, 1962.</ref>

:<math>y = x f\left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right) + g\left( \frac{dy}{dx}\right).</math>

After differentiating once, and rearranging with <math>p=dy/dx</math>, we have

:<math>\frac{dx}{dp} + \frac{x f'(p) + g'(p)}{f(p)-p}=0</math>

The above equation is a first order linear differential equation: 
:<math>\frac{dx}{dp} + \frac{f'(p)}{f(p)-p}x=\frac{- g'(p)}{f(p)-p}</math>
as the general form:
:<math>\frac{dx}{dp} + R(p) x=Q(p)</math>
When <math>f(p)=p</math>, d'Alembert's equation is reduced to [[Clairaut's equation]].
